lead: A coupler splits light into two or more arms, an isolator passes light one way only, a circulator sends light round a fixed 1→2→3 route, and a Bragg grating reflects one wavelength and passes the rest. None needs electrical power: they are passive. They set how much power a WDM link loses and how much of one channel leaks into its neighbour, so every WDM node is built from them.
prereq: You need total internal reflection and single-mode fiber from Unit 1, the back-reflection problem of laser diodes from Unit 3, and the WDM channel picture from 6.1.

sections.h3: Couplers: sharing light with no power supply

blocks.text: A coupler takes light in at one port and shares it among two or more output ports; run backwards, it combines several inputs into one output. Only glass is involved, so it needs no supply and never wears out.

The fused biconical taper (FBT) coupler is made by placing or twisting two single-mode fibers together, fusing the joint and tapering (stretching) it. Over the fused length the cores lie so close that light leaks from one core into the other. The planar coupler does the same with waveguides patterned on a silica substrate; coupling is fixed by waveguide spacing and length, so it drifts less with temperature.

Shapes include the 1×2 splitter, 2×2 coupler, N×N star that mixes many inputs into many outputs, and the tree built from 1×2 stages. Splitting costs power: a perfect 1×2 gives half to each arm, which is 3 dB.

items: Coupling ratio CR = P₃/(P₃ + P₄) × 100 percent: share of total output leaving one arm. A 50:50 coupler has CR = 50 percent.
Excess loss = 10 log₁₀(P<sub>in</sub>/(P₃ + P₄)) dB: power lost inside the coupler, found by adding all outputs.
Insertion loss = 10 log₁₀(P<sub>in</sub>/P₃) dB: loss from input to one chosen output port; it contains both split ratio and excess loss.

Directivity = 10 log₁₀(P<sub>3,forward</sub>/P<sub>1,leak</sub>) dB: P<sub>3,forward</sub> is the output at port 3 for light fed into port 1; P<sub>1,leak</sub> is the small power appearing at port 1 when light is fed into port 3. High directivity keeps echoes out of the link.
Uniformity = 10 log₁₀(P<sub>max</sub>/P<sub>min</sub>) dB over the output ports: how evenly a 1×N splitter shares power.

blocks.text: P<sub>in</sub> is input power at port 1; P₃ and P₄ are output powers, all in the same unit (mW or W). A power ratio in a log is dimensionless, so dB is the same with mW or W.
A laser diode is disturbed by light reflected back into it: the reflected wave pulls the gain and adds noise (Unit 3). An isolator is the one-way valve that stops it.

An isolator is a polarizer, a Faraday rotator and a second polarizer. The first polarizer passes one plane. The Faraday rotator, a magneto-optic crystal in a magnetic field, turns that plane by 45°; the second polarizer sits at 45° and passes the light. The key: the crystal rotates the plane in the same sense viewed from the lab, whatever the direction of travel. Light reflected from the fiber turns another 45°, arrives at 90° to the first polarizer, and is blocked.

A circulator is the three-port version: light in at port 1 leaves by port 2, in at port 2 leaves by port 3, in at port 3 leaves by port 1. The reverse route 2→1 is heavily attenuated. Because a circulator routes light instead of splitting it, no 3 dB is thrown away. That makes it the natural partner of a Bragg grating.

A fiber Bragg grating is a short piece of fiber whose core refractive index rises and falls periodically along the axis with pitch Λ. The forward wave reflects weakly at every period. Those reflections add in phase for one wavelength only, the Bragg wavelength.

blocks.where: λ_B is the reflected Bragg wavelength (m); n_eff is the effective index of the guided mode, about 1.45 in silica; Λ is the grating pitch (m). The factor 2 is the round trip: the wave travels one pitch forward and one pitch back.

blocks.text: All other wavelengths pass almost untouched, so the grating is a band-stop (notch) filter with bandwidth from a fraction of a nanometre to a few nanometres.

Apodization means tapering the modulation strength gradually to zero at the two ends. A sharp start and stop produce side lobes: small unwanted reflection peaks just outside the main reflected band, sitting right on neighbouring WDM channels. Tapering removes them.
Uses: notch filter in front of a pump laser, a WDM demultiplexer (a chain of gratings, each reflecting one channel), gain flattening, and chirped gratings for dispersion compensation.

With a circulator the grating becomes an add-drop multiplexer. Channels λ1 to λ4 enter port 1 and leave at port 2, where the grating reflects λ2 back; λ1, λ3 and λ4 pass straight through to the output line, and the reflected λ2 re-enters port 2 and leaves at port 3 as the dropped channel. To add a channel, feed the new λ2 into port 3; the circulator sends it back along the same reflection path.

Thin-film filters do the same in free space: a stack of dielectric layers, each a quarter-wave thick at the design wavelength, on glass. Reflections at layer boundaries add for one band and cancel for the rest. A demultiplexer is a chain of such filters, each dropping one channel. A tunable Fabry-Perot filter is a cavity between two mirrors; it passes a comb of wavelengths, and moving the mirrors slides the comb so one channel is chosen.

figure.caption: Light entering port 1 of the circulator leaves at port 2 and reaches the grating. The grating reflects λ2 back into port 2, so the circulator sends it out at port 3 as the dropped channel; λ1 and λ3 pass through the grating to the output line.

spec.title: Circulator plus grating as an add-drop node

examples.question: A fused 2×2 coupler receives 1.00 mW at port 1. Ports 3 and 4 each give 0.40 mW. (a) Find the coupling ratio. (b) Find the excess loss. (c) Find the insertion loss of one output port. (d) Find the grating pitch that reflects 1550 nm in a fiber with n_eff = 1.45.
steps: (a) Total output = P₃ + P₄ = 0.40 + 0.40 = 0.80 mW. CR = P₃/(P₃ + P₄) × 100 = 0.40/0.80 × 100 = 50 percent, a 50:50 coupler.
(b) Excess loss = 10 log₁₀(P<sub>in</sub>/(P₃ + P₄)) = 10 log₁₀(1.00/0.80) = 10 log₁₀(1.25) = 10 × 0.0969 = 0.97 dB.
(c) Insertion loss = 10 log₁₀(P<sub>in</sub>/P₃) = 10 log₁₀(1.00/0.40) = 10 log₁₀(2.5) = 10 × 0.3979 = 3.98 dB.
Check: 3.98 dB is close to the ideal 3.01 dB of a 50:50 split plus the 0.97 dB excess loss.
examples.answer: CR = 50:50, excess loss = 0.97 dB, insertion loss = 3.98 dB, grating pitch = 534.48 nm.
examples.check:
import math
Pin = 1.00e-3
P3 = 0.40e-3
P4 = 0.40e-3
cr = P3/(P3+P4)*100
excess = 10*math.log10(Pin/(P3+P4))
il = 10*math.log10(Pin/P3)
pitch = 1550/(2*1.45)
print(round(cr,2))
print(round(excess,2))
print(round(il,2))
print(round(pitch,2))

traps: Dropping the factor 2 in λ_B = 2 n_eff Λ. The wave goes one pitch forward and one back, so the 2 is always there; without it the pitch comes out double.
Treating excess loss and insertion loss as the same number. Excess loss compares total output with input; insertion loss compares one port with input.
Measuring the coupling ratio against the input power instead of total output power. CR is a share of what comes out.
Swapping isolation and insertion loss on an isolator. Isolation is the reverse attenuation (40 to 60 dB); insertion loss is the small forward penalty (0.5 to 1 dB).
Assuming a circulator splits power like a coupler. It routes full power in one fixed direction, which is why it wastes no 3 dB.

quiz.q: Define excess loss of a coupler and write its formula.
quiz.a: Excess loss is the power lost inside the coupler, found by adding all output powers and comparing with the input: excess loss = 10 log₁₀(P_in/(P₃ + P₄)) dB.

quiz.q: State the Bragg condition for a fiber grating and name each symbol.
quiz.a: λ_B = 2 n_eff Λ, where λ_B is the reflected wavelength, n_eff the effective mode index (about 1.45 in silica) and Λ the grating pitch.

quiz.q: Why does an isolator block the reverse path but pass the forward path, when the Faraday rotator turns light by 45° either way?
quiz.a: The Faraday rotation has the same sense in the lab for both directions. Forward light leaves the rotator at 45° and the second polarizer, set at 45°, passes it. Reflected light starts at 45°, is turned another 45° to 90°, and now meets the first polarizer crossed, so it is absorbed.

quiz.q: A 1×2 coupler gets 2.0 mW at port 1; ports 3 and 4 each give 0.90 mW. Find the coupling ratio, the excess loss and the insertion loss at one port.
A Bragg grating must reflect 1310 nm in a fiber with n_eff = 1.447. Find the pitch.
A grating used inside a WDM demultiplexer has strong side lobes. Explain the cause and the cure, and say what happens to the neighbouring channels without the cure.
quiz.a: A grating whose modulation starts and stops abruptly behaves like a rectangular window; its reflection spectrum shows side lobes just outside the main reflected band. Those lobes reflect a small part of the next WDM channel, giving crosstalk. Apodization, tapering the modulation slowly to zero at both ends, suppresses the side lobes at the cost of a slightly longer grating.

quiz.q: Explain how a circulator and a Bragg grating together form an add-drop multiplexer, and why a 2×2 coupler is a poorer choice for the same node.
quiz.a: Light enters circulator port 1 and leaves at port 2 into the grating. The grating reflects only λ2; the other channels pass to the output line. The reflected λ2 returns to port 2 and the circulator sends it out at port 3 as the dropped channel. Adding works along the same reflection path. A 2×2 coupler would split each channel in both directions, losing at least 3 dB per pass, and would also send part of every other channel into the drop port, adding crosstalk.

beyond: Not for the exam. On real boards these parts are no longer separate: planar lightwave circuits put couplers, splitters and switches on one silica or silicon chip. Arrayed waveguide gratings, a chain of planar couplers and waveguides, do the multiplexing job that a stack of thin-film filters does. Fiber Bragg gratings also serve as strain and temperature sensors, because pitch Λ stretches with the fiber and the reflected wavelength shifts measurably. Search for planar lightwave circuits, arrayed waveguide grating and fiber Bragg grating sensors to go further.
